conclusions: The source defines this system to be hyperbolic precisely by the existence of a full set of m linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to real eigenvalues of A. In explicit linear-algebra notation, this means there exist lambda^1,...,lambda^m in R and linearly independent r^1,...,r^m in R^m with A r^p = lambda^p r^p for every p = 1,...,m. This notation unpacks the defining sentence rather than introducing a separate source theorem. Locations: raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening paragraph; raw PDF page 69, printed page 47, recall of real diagonalizability and right eigenvectors.

ambiguities.evidence: Raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, describes m as the number of unknown components and identifies m = 1 as the simplest scalar case. Raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, requires m independent eigenvectors, without discussing an empty system or m = 0.
ambiguities.impact: The intended PDE examples have positive dimension, but the selected passage supplies no explicit zero-dimensional convention. A formal extension to m = 0 should be identified as such instead of being presented as an expressly stated source case.

contract_plain_english: For the one-dimensional homogeneous linear system q_t + A q_x = 0, where q takes values in R^m and A is a constant real m × m matrix, hyperbolicity is defined by A admitting a full real eigenvector basis with real associated eigenvalues. Relative to any such selected basis, every vector in R^m has unique expansion coefficients. The eigenvalues are the propagation speeds of the corresponding wave components. The source imposes no distinctness or sign restriction on those eigenvalues and does not restrict the definition to the motivating two-component acoustics example. Sources: raw PDF page 23, printed page 1, equation (1.1) and its description; raw PDF page 25, printed page 3, opening defining paragraph; raw PDF pages 69–70, printed pages 47–48, equations (3.2)–(3.6) and their explanations. The treatment of dimension zero is not explicit in these passages.
